name: E-Commerce Use Case
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Blockchain in Your Shopping Cart: Mostly Marketing, Occasionally Real
lesson.summary: E-commerce blockchain projects split cleanly into two piles: narrow, still-operating uses like luxury goods authentication, and flashier consumer-facing plays like decentralized marketplaces and loyalty tokens that mostly failed to attract lasting real usage.
lesson.body:
E-commerce blockchain pitches usually promise some combination of the same benefits: reducing counterfeit goods, removing middlemen and their fees through decentralized marketplaces, tokenized loyalty programs that work across many different brands, and faster cross-border payments. Applying the case-study-analysis checklist to each of these separately produces noticeably different verdicts.

Luxury goods authentication is the strongest of the group. The AURA Blockchain Consortium, founded by LVMH around 2021 with technology from Consensys and Microsoft and later joined by Prada Group and Cartier's parent company Richemont, lets a shopper verify a luxury item's authenticity and ownership history through a digital record tied to the physical product. This is a genuinely plausible use case, because counterfeiting is a real and expensive problem for these brands. But it is worth being precise about what kind of trust is actually being established: the brand itself is already the trusted authority on whether its own product is genuine, so the real question a skeptic should ask is whether this is a case where a centralized brand-run database, tied to a serial number and a phone app, would provide nearly the same consumer benefit without the overhead of a shared ledger. Public information about current usage scale for AURA is limited, so it is worth treating claims about its reach with the same caution recommended in the case-study-analysis chapter.

Decentralized marketplaces make the opposite case even more clearly. OpenBazaar, launched in the mid-2010s, aimed to be a peer-to-peer alternative to eBay or Amazon with no central platform, no listing fees, and no company controlling the marketplace. It never reached meaningful scale and effectively wound down. The lesson is not that decentralization failed technically, but that most buyers and sellers actually want the things a centralized platform provides more than they want to avoid its fee: dispute resolution when an order goes wrong, buyer protection, search and discovery, seller reputation, and someone accountable when something breaks. "Removing the middleman" turned out to badly undersell how much real value the middleman was providing.

Blockchain-based loyalty and rewards tokens followed a similar arc. Various retailers and startups launched programs between roughly 2018 and 2021 promising loyalty points that could move across brands, redeem Starbucks points toward a Delta flight, for instance, using tokens on a shared ledger instead of each company's isolated points database. Almost none of these reached meaningful adoption. Ordinary loyalty programs, which are just points tracked in each retailer's own database, already work fine for the overwhelming majority of customers, and the cross-brand benefit blockchain promised rarely had enough participating brands actually signed up to matter in practice.

Running all three through the same lens this chapter has used throughout, and connecting back to the blockchain definition, the pattern is consistent: the one case with a real, ongoing multi-party trust problem (verifying authenticity across a brand's own supply chain and resale market) has some staying power, while the cases pitched mainly as "no middleman needed" turned out to be solving a problem that was never really the customer's biggest pain point.
